caveats.text: Every map, outline and rotation here comes from one reconstruction, Scotese’s PALEOMAP atlas (2016). Other published reconstructions place the continents differently, and the uncertainty grows with age, because the ocean floor that recorded older plate motions has mostly been lost to subduction.
caveats.title: One reconstruction among several

caveats.text: The land and shallow-sea figures and the readout’s “what was there” come from Scotese and Wright’s elevation models, which their report calls a “first draft” (p. 7).
caveats.title: Elevations are a first draft

caveats.text: Magnetism frozen in rocks records how far from the pole they formed, not their longitude, so east–west positions on the older maps are less certain than north–south ones.
caveats.title: Longitude is the weak coordinate

caveats.text: Temperature and rain come from a climate model (HadCM3L), not from measurements: one run per 5 million years, each averaged over its last 100 model years and driven by a carbon dioxide history. Temperature is the air’s, 1.5 m (5 ft) above the surface, over land and sea alike; rain includes snow. Its pre-industrial world averages 58.5 °F (14.7 °C); the tiles compare with that, not with a thermometer record.
caveats.title: Temperature and rain are a model

caveats.text: Older than 419.5 million years ago the curve is the carbon dioxide the climate model was run with, a model input, not a fit to measurements. The band drawn is Foster’s 68% band; his 95% band is left out because its lower edge falls below zero in 124 rows between 247 and 419.5 million years ago.
caveats.title: Carbon dioxide before 419.5 million years

caveats.text: Map ages are Scotese’s, on the 2008 timescale his atlas uses. Names and colors come from today’s ICS chart (version 2026-06); for 11 maps Scotese’s label and today’s chart disagree on a boundary or a period, and the sheet says so for each.
caveats.title: Two timescales

caveats.text: Arrows and speeds are the rotation model’s motion over the million years before each map. Overlays are rotated to the map’s own time, which differs from its printed age by up to 4 million years. Between maps the app cross-fades; it never draws an Earth between two of the 90 maps.
caveats.title: Motion and fades

caveats.text: Crust the model holds only for today covers 62.7% of the globe, 99.8% of it under today’s oceans. A city or a tap on it has no position on older maps.
caveats.title: Today’s ocean floor has no past here

caveats.text: The Sun tile evaluates Gough’s (1981) formula for the young Sun’s slow brightening; at 750 million years ago it gives 94% of today’s brightness.
caveats.title: The Sun

caveats.text: The colors of the Temperature and Rain lenses, the globe’s shading, the bright rim at its edge, its glow, the night behind it and the frame around the view are display choices, not data.
caveats.title: Display choices

intro: Earth’s History shows the planet at 90 moments from 750 million years ago to today, one per map in C. R. Scotese’s PALEOMAP PaleoAtlas. The maps are a reconstruction, the temperature and rain a climate model, the curves published fits; each is labeled as what it is. The cards and events were written for this app from 47 published sources, cited beside the text. Nothing is fetched: every file ships inside the app.

not_shown.text: Plate boundaries: no open set exists for Scotese’s model, and other models’ ridges and trenches belong with their own continents, so drawing them here would mix two reconstructions. Anything older than 750 million years beyond a short text: no map exists. The continents between maps: that would be invented geography. Seasons, sea temperature and salinity: the app shows annual air temperature and rain. Oxygen and biodiversity curves: no openly licensed series was found. Climate for the maps at 600, 690 and 750 million years ago: no model run. Plate names: the model has codes, not names. Ocean names: an ocean is not a plate, so there is nothing to pin a name to. Relief in 3D, and zoom beyond the maps’ detail.
not_shown.title: What this app does not show, and why

reading.text: The Surface lens shows Scotese’s 90 maps, about 6 million years apart back to 542 million years ago and then only at 600, 690 and 750 million years ago. Each was drawn from the rock record where it survives and inferred from the region’s tectonic history where it does not (atlas pp. 4–5). His color key (pp. 7–8): dark blue deep ocean, light blue shelves and flooded continents, green lowlands, tan plateaus and foothills, brown mountains, white the highest peaks.
reading.title: The painted maps

reading.text: These lenses show a climate model’s annual means from 109 runs, one every 5 million years back to 540 million years ago, each on Scotese’s geography; a map uses the run nearest its age. The maps at 600, 690 and 750 million years ago have no run, and the lenses say so.
reading.title: Temperature and Rain

reading.text: Plates outlines pieces of today’s crust in Scotese’s plate model, 503 outlines on 241 plates, where the model puts them at each map’s time; arrows show how they moved over the million years before it. These are pieces of today’s crust, not plate boundaries.
reading.title: Plates

reading.text: Today’s coastlines, the cities in Find and the Look-for pins are stored where they are now and carried back with the plate they sit on. Where the model does not carry that crust back to a map’s age, nothing is drawn and the readout says so.
reading.title: Today’s coasts, cities and pins

reading.text: The strip under the slider shows the climate model’s global mean temperature, carbon dioxide (Foster and colleagues’ fit to proxy measurements back to 419.5 million years ago, then the model’s input, dashed) and sea level relative to today (back to 540 million years ago). The tiles compare each map with today in the same source: the model’s own pre-industrial world at 58.5 °F (14.7 °C), the same curve at 0 Ma, and the same elevation model’s 27.6% land.
reading.title: Curves and tiles

sources.accuracy: A painted reconstruction by one author: one interpretation among several. Map ages are Scotese's Table 1 ages on the 2008 timescale his atlas uses. Rotations reproduce pygplates within 0.36 km after 16-bit rounding. Rotations are one model's reconstruction; beyond each plate's last pole the rotation file holds the pole constant.
sources.adaptations: Maps: resized from 3600 x 1800 to 1024 x 512 (Lanczos) and re-encoded as WebP quality 65; a 256 x 128 preview of each, combined into one sheet at quality 70. No colors or content changed. Plate model: the 503 polygon outlines stored at their 0 Ma positions with coordinates rounded to 16 bits; the rotation of each of the 241 plates at each map's time and one million years earlier, as 16-bit quaternions; the 2 line features in the polygon file left out.

sources.accuracy: The readout names the class of the nearest 2-degree node, which can be up to about 1.4 degrees of arc from the point tapped. The authors call these elevation models a first draft.
sources.adaptations: Elevation classes: Every second node of each 1-degree grid (a 2-degree grid) sorted into the ten elevation classes of Scotese's Table 2 (after Ziegler et al. 1985) and stored as one byte per node; the elevations themselves are not shipped. Land and shallow-sea area: Land (above 0 m) and shallow sea (0 to 200 m deep) as shares of the globe, weighted by the cosine of latitude, one value per grid.

sources.accuracy: A climate model, not measurements: one HadCM3L run per 5 million years on Scotese's reconstructed geography, forced with a CO2 history. Byte rounding changes values by at most 0.25 C and 0.060 mm/day. Model output and a model input, not measurements.
sources.adaptations: Climate fields: Averaged over the 12 months and the five 20-year means into annual means; temperature converted from kelvin to degrees Celsius and precipitation from kg m-2 s-1 to mm/day; each value rounded to one byte (temperature in steps of 0.5 C, rain on a square-root scale); area-weighted global means computed. Curves: Global mean temperature and the CO2 input interpolated linearly between the 5-million-year runs.

sources.adaptations: The app evaluates equation (1) with the Sun's main-sequence age of 4.7 billion years at each map's age; nothing is stored.

sources.source: Equation (1), p. 28: L(t) = [1 + 2/5 (1 - t/t_sun)]^-1 L_sun for t <= t_sun, with the Main-Sequence age t_sun "about 4.7 x 10^9 yr" (p. 23). Read from the NASA ADS scan https://articles.adsabs.harvard.edu/pdf/1981SoPh...74...21G (publisher copyright; the formula is used, no text or figure is copied).
